title: Overview
heading: Overview
text: Infrayard is a self-service portal for Oracle Kubernetes Engine (OKE). Engineers create, scale, upgrade and delete OKE clusters through a web portal. Platform administrators decide which templates, sizes and Kubernetes versions are allowed, and approve protected operations. Behind the portal, Terraform creates the resources in your own OCI tenancy. You install Infrayard in your environment: on an OKE cluster, or on k3s on a single VM for an evaluation. Credentials, state and data stay with you.

title: Overview
heading: What Infrayard does
text: Clusters: create, scale, upgrade and destroy OKE clusters (Basic and Enhanced), with live Terraform logs. Access: one-click kubeconfig per user, without OCI CLI setup. Guardrails: templates, per-user resource limits, protected destroy requests and limit-increase requests. Visibility: Activity inbox, audit log and cost estimates before deployment. Existing infrastructure: use your own compartments, VCNs and subnets. Application deployment and day-to-day workload operations stay in your existing tools. See the product scope .

title: Overview
heading: How to get started
text: Request a demo to see a real workflow and discuss your environment. Check the requirements . Start a subscription or an evaluation, receive your registry access and install . The releases and roadmap page separates what is available today from planned work.

title: Architecture
heading: Overview
text: Infrayard runs in an environment you control: an OKE cluster, or k3s on a single VM. There is no Solvia Lab cloud service in between. Infrayard works in your OCI tenancy with its own OCI user and keeps its data in your database and your Object Storage bucket.

title: Architecture
heading: Components
text: Component What it does Runs as Portal Web interface: clusters, requests, access downloads, administration infrayard-frontend (nginx) API Checks tokens and requests, stores data, starts and tracks Terraform jobs infrayard-api Terraform runner Runs provisioning, scale, upgrade and destroy jobs Inside infrayard-api PostgreSQL Clusters, jobs, users, configuration, templates, requests, audit log infrayard-postgresql , or your external PostgreSQL Keycloak Sign-in, users and roles infrayard-keycloak , or your existing Keycloak Object Storage bucket Terraform state of every managed cluster In your OCI tenancy OCI and OKE The cloud resources themselves Your OCI tenancy The Helm chart installs these services. An ingress controller in your cluster, such as Traefik, terminates HTTPS in front of the portal. The portal and the bundled Keycloak share one address: the portal at https://infrayard.example.com , Keycloak at https://infrayard.example.com/auth . The portal forwards /api to the API and /auth to Keycloak; the Keycloak admin console is not reachable this way.

title: Architecture
heading: What happens when a user creates a cluster
text: The user signs in through Keycloak and receives a token. The portal shows the templates, options and limits that apply to this user. The API checks the request: limits, template, compatibility of version, shape and image, and network settings. The API starts a Terraform job with the Infrayard OCI user. Terraform stores the cluster's state in the bucket. The portal streams the Terraform log. When the job ends, the cluster status, Activity entry and audit record are updated. For a running cluster, the API creates a per-user ServiceAccount in the cluster and issues the kubeconfig. Destroy requests and requests for higher limits go through the administrator review. Other operations run immediately within the user's limits.

title: Architecture
heading: State and ownership
text: PostgreSQL holds the platform data; the bucket holds the Terraform state. Back up both and keep them consistent; see operations . Resources created by Infrayard are managed by their cluster's Terraform state, and manual changes are overwritten by the next run. Existing networks you supply are only referenced; see networking .

title: Architecture
heading: Connections
text: From To Why Users Portal (443) Use Infrayard and sign in API OCI APIs and Object Storage (443) Create and inspect resources, Terraform state API Kubernetes API of managed clusters (6443) Issue kubeconfigs API Keycloak Fetch the realm's signing keys Host Image registry (443) Pull the Infrayard images API, optional SMTP server E-mail notifications The installation needs no inbound connection from the internet when users come through a VPN. See private access .

title: Architecture
heading: Operating responsibility
text: You operate the installation, its database, secrets, storage and network, and the workloads on your clusters. Oracle provides OCI and OKE. Solvia Lab provides the Infrayard releases, documentation and the support defined in your agreement.

text: Sign-in uses Keycloak: either the Keycloak bundled with Infrayard (realm, client and admin role are created automatically) or a realm in your existing Keycloak 22 or newer. See Use your own Keycloak .

title: Requirements and compatibility
heading: Costs outside the subscription
text: The subscription covers the Infrayard software. Your Oracle Cloud bill covers the OKE clusters and their nodes, load balancers and storage, and the host that runs Infrayard: capacity and one block volume in your cluster (50 GB on OKE, the OCI minimum) plus a load balancer for the ingress, or the VM for k3s.

title: Requirements and compatibility
heading: OKE versions, shapes and images
text: Which Kubernetes versions, shapes and node images exist depends on your region and tenancy. Administrators sync them from OCI in Admin → Configuration and enable what users may choose. Newly synced Kubernetes versions stay disabled until an administrator enables them. The deploy and template forms only offer Kubernetes versions that have a node image for the selected shape. If Infrayard cannot check this with OCI, deployment is blocked rather than allowing an unverified combination. See troubleshooting .

title: Requirements and compatibility
heading: Basic and Enhanced clusters
text: The platform can allow Basic, Enhanced or both OKE cluster types. These are Oracle service tiers, separate from Infrayard subscription plans. Operation Basic Enhanced Add or remove nodes and pools Automatic Automatic Change a pool's shape, OCPUs, memory or storage Needs rolling worker cycling Automatic rollout Kubernetes upgrade Control plane first, then a rolling worker refresh Automatic control plane and worker rollout OCI control-plane charges Oracle's Basic pricing Oracle's Enhanced pricing See cluster lifecycle for the steps.

title: Requirements and compatibility
heading: Product scope
text: Infrayard provisions and manages OKE clusters: create, access, scale, upgrade and destroy, with templates, limits, requests, cost estimates, audit records and existing-network support. Deploying applications, CI/CD and application databases stay in your existing tools. Running Infrayard on an existing OKE cluster is different from managing that cluster with Infrayard. Infrayard manages only clusters it created; existing clusters are not imported. One installation manages one anchor compartment tree. Unrelated trees need the tenancy root as anchor or separate installations. Existing subnets need their VCN as well, and prepared routing. The public API endpoint mode needs Infrayard-managed networking. AI assistance, an access agent and non-OCI clouds are on the roadmap , not in the product today. Running in your tenancy does not by itself make the setup compliant, highly available or air-gapped.

title: Security and access
heading: Overview
text: Infrayard runs entirely in your environment. OCI credentials, Terraform state, the database and logs stay with you; there is no Solvia Lab cloud service in the path, and Infrayard sends no data to Solvia Lab.

title: Security and access
heading: Identity and roles
text: Sign-in uses OpenID Connect with the Authorization Code flow and PKCE, handled by Keycloak: the one bundled with Infrayard or a realm in your existing Keycloak. The portal is a public client, so no client secret is stored in the browser. The API checks the signature, issuer and audience of every token. Infrayard creates a user record on the first sign-in. Access is controlled by Keycloak roles or groups: Admin role : the administration area, all clusters, users, configuration, templates, requests and audit log. Access role (optional): only users with it may sign in. Use it with a shared company realm. Template roles : a template can require a role, so only some users see it. When a role is removed or the Keycloak session ends, the user is signed out within a few minutes. Details: Use your own Keycloak .

title: Security and access
heading: OCI credentials
text: Infrayard acts in OCI as one service user with an API key. Its policies are scoped to the anchor compartment; read access covers the tenancy so that regions, shapes and networks can be listed. See Prepare OCI . Where the credentials are stored: Secret Where OCI API private key Secret infrayard-oci-key , mounted read-only into the API S3 key for the state bucket, database and Keycloak passwords Secrets created by the chart from your values Keep these in your secret manager. Never send them in support requests. Rotating the API key: add a new key to the OCI user, update the secret and the fingerprint, roll out, then delete the old key in OCI.

title: Security and access
heading: Kubernetes access
text: Users download a kubeconfig from a running cluster's detail page. It works with plain kubectl , without the OCI CLI: export KUBECONFIG=~/Downloads/oke-my-cluster-kubeconfig.yaml kubectl get nodes How it works: Each Infrayard user gets their own ServiceAccount in the namespace infrayard-system of the cluster, so Kubernetes audit logs show the actual person. The ServiceAccount is bound to cluster-admin . Everyone who may download a kubeconfig for a cluster has full rights on it. The embedded token is valid for up to 30 days; the cluster may shorten that. Download a new kubeconfig when it expires. To revoke a user's access to a cluster at once, delete their ServiceAccount: kubectl delete serviceaccount <user> -n infrayard-system . Users with an OCI CLI setup can download an alternative kubeconfig that authenticates through the OCI CLI. Cluster owners download access for their clusters; administrators can download it for every cluster in All Clusters → Details . Include this in your access review. The kubeconfig does not create a network path. Users need a route to the cluster's API endpoint; see networking .

title: Security and access
heading: SSH access
text: Terraform generates an SSH key pair for each cluster's worker nodes. The private key is stored in the Infrayard database and can be downloaded from the cluster's detail page. Treat it as a credential, and treat database backups as sensitive for this reason.

title: Security and access
heading: Audit and approvals
text: Every lifecycle operation records who did what, on which cluster, the result and the duration. Destroy requests and limit-increase requests record the submission and the decision. Administrators can force-destroy a cluster for incident response; this is recorded too. The Activity inbox shows lifecycle events, request outcomes and limit changes. Optional e-mail notifications send event details to the configured recipients through your SMTP server.

title: Security and access
heading: Network exposure
text: The portal is the only inbound endpoint. The Keycloak admin console is not exposed: it is reached with kubectl port-forward . We recommend making the portal reachable only from your VPN . Outbound, Infrayard needs OCI APIs, the image registry and the cluster APIs; see requirements .

title: Security and access
heading: Hardening built in
text: The Infrayard, Keycloak and PostgreSQL containers run as non-root users and drop all Linux capabilities; the API and the portal also use read-only root file systems. The portal sends security headers ( X-Content-Type-Options , X-Frame-Options , Referrer-Policy , Permissions-Policy ) and redirects HTTP to HTTPS. Configuration or secret changes roll the affected pods automatically on helm upgrade .

title: Security and access
heading: Your security review
text: Before production, review TLS and exposure, OCI policy scope, who holds the admin role, kubeconfig rights, secret storage, database and state backups, and log access. Security questionnaires and additional evidence can be arranged through Enterprise .

title: Networking and existing infrastructure
heading: Overview
text: Each cluster needs a network, and its Kubernetes API must be reachable from Infrayard and from your users. This page explains what Infrayard creates by default, how to reuse your own VCNs, subnets and compartments, and which access mode to choose for the Kubernetes API.

title: Networking and existing infrastructure
heading: Default setup
text: Without any overrides, Infrayard creates a complete network for every cluster, in the cluster's own compartment: A VCN whose /16 range is derived from the cluster's /24 CIDR. A private worker subnet (/24). Worker nodes have no public IPs. A public load balancer subnet for Kubernetes LoadBalancer services. A public API endpoint subnet , only in the restricted public API mode (below). Internet, NAT and service gateways with route tables. Security lists with the rules OKE needs, plus the TCP/6443 allowlist for the API. All of it belongs to the cluster's Terraform state and is removed when the cluster is destroyed.

title: Networking and existing infrastructure
heading: Kubernetes API endpoint access
text: Choose the mode in Admin → Configuration → OCI Settings → Kubernetes API Access : the box Public endpoint restricted by CIDR allowlist and the list Allowed API CIDRs . The setting applies to clusters created afterwards. Mode Where the API is Who can reach it Private endpoint (box off, default) Private subnet, no public IP Anything with a route into the VCN: VPN through a DRG, FastConnect, a bastion, or Infrayard running in a peered network Public endpoint restricted by CIDR allowlist Dedicated public subnet Only the CIDR ranges you list; 0.0.0.0/0 is rejected With Public endpoint restricted by CIDR allowlist on, list both in Allowed API CIDRs : your VPN or office egress ranges, so users can run kubectl , and the outbound address of Infrayard itself (NAT gateway or VM public IP), because Infrayard calls the cluster API to issue kubeconfigs. This mode avoids routing every cluster VCN to your network, which helps when DRG attachments are costly or local peering limits are reached. Users still connect from the VPN or office network. The kubeconfig only provides authentication. Without a network path to port 6443, kubectl times out.

title: Networking and existing infrastructure
heading: Bringing your own network
text: In the deploy form, the Advanced tab accepts existing OCIDs. Infrayard then skips creating those resources: Field Effect Existing Compartment OCID Resources go into this compartment instead of a new one Existing VCN OCID Uses your VCN; Infrayard creates only the cluster subnets and their security lists inside it Existing Subnet OCID Worker nodes go into your subnet; requires the VCN OCID as well Supported combinations: You provide Infrayard creates and manages Nothing Compartment, VCN, subnets, gateways, route tables, security lists, cluster Compartment VCN and the complete network inside that compartment, cluster VCN (optionally compartment) Subnets and security lists in your VCN, cluster. Your gateways and route tables are used as they are VCN and subnet (optionally compartment) Only the cluster and node pools. Your network is used read-only Subnet without VCN Rejected before Terraform starts Rules: Stay inside the anchor. A supplied compartment must be the anchor compartment or any compartment below it. Others are rejected before Terraform starts, because the OCI policies only cover the anchor subtree. No automatic discovery. Supplying only a compartment does not reuse a VCN that already exists in it; Infrayard creates a new one. Routing must be ready. With your own VCN or subnet, the worker subnet needs a route 0.0.0.0/0 to a NAT gateway (or your egress path) and a route for all-<region>-services-in-oracle-services-network to a service gateway. Otherwise nodes cannot register. Public endpoint restricted by CIDR allowlist needs an Infrayard-managed VCN. While this mode is on, deployments with an existing VCN or subnet are rejected; an existing compartment is fine. Sharing a compartment: to place several clusters in one compartment, create a compartment for them and supply it to each cluster. Do not reuse a compartment that Infrayard created for another cluster. The OCID fields check the OCID type and offer autocomplete lists of the compartments, VCNs and subnets Infrayard can see.

title: Networking and existing infrastructure
heading: Choosing the anchor compartment
text: The anchor is set at installation and can be changed in Admin → Configuration . Typical choices: Anchor Good for Note A dedicated compartment, e.g. infrayard Clear separation and the narrowest permissions Existing networks must be inside it An existing compartment such as platform Reusing networks and compartments that already exist there The policies grant management of everything below it The tenancy root Reusing anything in the tenancy Policies at tenancy scope; widest permissions One installation cannot span several unrelated compartment trees. Use the tenancy root as anchor, or run separate installations.

title: Networking and existing infrastructure
heading: Who owns what
text: Resources Infrayard creates are managed by the cluster's Terraform state. Manual changes in the OCI Console are overwritten by the next scale or upgrade. Resources you supply (compartment, VCN, subnet) are only referenced, never changed or deleted.

title: Networking and existing infrastructure
heading: Custom security rules
text: The default security lists cover what OKE needs. For your own rules, for example extra node ports, restricted egress or network security groups, supply your own subnet with those rules already in place. Infrayard then creates no security list of its own.

title: Installation
heading: Overview
text: Infrayard runs on a Kubernetes cluster in your environment: an OKE cluster for production, or k3s on a single VM for an evaluation. Both use the same Helm chart, images and values. Installation takes about an hour, including the OCI preparation.

title: Installation
heading: Choose your deployment path
text: Existing OKE cluster Other Kubernetes (k3s, …) Good for Production Evaluation on a single VM, or production Installed with Helm chart Helm chart Ingress and TLS Your ingress controller (e.g. Traefik) and cert-manager Same; k3s ships Traefik Database storage OCI Block Volume ( oci-bv ), 50 GB Your StorageClass (k3s: local-path ) Keycloak Bundled or your own Bundled or your own Guide Install on Kubernetes Install on Kubernetes For an evaluation , one VM with k3s is enough. We recommend 2 OCPUs and 8 GB RAM. At idle, the full stack used about 2.7 GiB on the Arm test VM and about 3.5 GB on an earlier demo VM. The four Infrayard pods on the Arm VM used about 0.85 GiB. The images run on x86 and Arm shapes. Prepare a k3s VM Both paths run one replica of each service, and Kubernetes restarts a service that fails. Neither is a high-availability setup for the portal itself. Your OKE clusters keep running if Infrayard is down.

title: Installation
heading: What you receive
text: When your order is accepted and the first invoice is paid, or when your evaluation starts, your technical contact receives an onboarding e-mail with: Item Value Registry user and token Personal to your organisation; the token can only pull Registry registry.gitlab.com Helm chart oci://registry.gitlab.com/solvialab/infrayard/charts/infrayard Images registry.gitlab.com/solvialab/infrayard/api and registry.gitlab.com/solvialab/infrayard/frontend Version to install A number such as 1.0.0 ; chart and images share it Support support@infrayard.eu The guides on this site are written so that your team can install Infrayard with these values on its own. Nothing is downloaded from a public website: the chart and the images come only from this registry. The token reads the registry and nothing else, for the term of your subscription or evaluation. Store it in your secret manager and ask support for a new one if it leaks.

title: Installation
heading: From the e-mail to the first cluster
text: Prepare OCI , about 20 minutes: the service user, policies, API key, state bucket and S3 key. Needed for every path. Prepare the host. Use an existing OKE cluster or prepare a k3s VM . Install with Helm , about 30 minutes, including DNS and the certificate. Configure and test: sign in, set up Admin → Configuration and create a test cluster, as in step 7 of the guide . The test cluster proves the OCI policies, the state bucket and the network path to the cluster API. Give people access: add users in the bundled Keycloak, or connect your own Keycloak . Recommended: make the portal reachable only from your VPN . Before production use: schedule the daily database backup and read how to upgrade . If a step fails, look it up in troubleshooting . If that does not help, write to support with the details listed there.
