title: Installation
heading: Prepare a k3s VM
text: This evaluation setup uses one public Oracle Linux 9 VM with 2 OCPUs and 8 GB RAM. The steps below were tested on Ampere Arm ( VM.Standard.A1.Flex ) with the bundled k3s Traefik. Use the tenancy and anchor compartment from the OCI setup and an OCI CLI profile with permission to create Compute and network resources. Prepare OCI

title: Installation
heading: Create the VM and its network in OCI
text: Run these commands in Bash with the OCI CLI and jq . Set T and C to your tenancy and compartment OCIDs, and replace the example SSH source with the public IPv4 address of your workstation or VPN. export OCI_CLI_REGION=eu-frankfurt-1 T=ocid1.tenancy.oc1..aaaa... C=ocid1.compartment.oc1..aaaa... SSH_CIDR=203.0.113.10/32 NAME=infrayard-k3s umask 077 mkdir -m 700 infrayard-host cd infrayard-host ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f ssh_ed25519 VCN=$(oci network vcn create -c "$C" --display-name "$NAME-vcn" \ --cidr-block 10.180.0.0/16 --wait-for-state AVAILABLE --query data.id --raw-output) IGW=$(oci network internet-gateway create -c "$C" --vcn-id "$VCN" \ --display-name "$NAME-igw" --is-enabled true \ --wait-for-state AVAILABLE --query data.id --raw-output) ROUTES=$(jq -nc --arg gateway "$IGW" \ '[{destination:"0.0.0.0/0",destinationType:"CIDR_BLOCK",networkEntityId:$gateway}]') RT=$(oci network route-table create -c "$C" --vcn-id "$VCN" \ --display-name "$NAME-rt" --route-rules "$ROUTES" \ --wait-for-state AVAILABLE --query data.id --raw-output) INGRESS=$(jq -nc --arg ssh "$SSH_CIDR" '[ {source:$ssh,protocol:"6",tcpOptions:{destinationPortRange:{min:22,max:22}}}, {source:"0.0.0.0/0",protocol:"6",tcpOptions:{destinationPortRange:{min:80,max:80}}}, {source:"0.0.0.0/0",protocol:"6",tcpOptions:{destinationPortRange:{min:443,max:443}}} ]') SL=$(oci network security-list create -c "$C" --vcn-id "$VCN" \ --display-name "$NAME-sl" --ingress-security-rules "$INGRESS" \ --egress-security-rules '[{"destination":"0.0.0.0/0","protocol":"all"}]' \ --wait-for-state AVAILABLE --query data.id --raw-output) SUBNET=$(oci network subnet create -c "$C" --vcn-id "$VCN" \ --display-name "$NAME-subnet" --cidr-block 10.180.1.0/24 \ --route-table-id "$RT" --security-list-ids "$(jq -nc --arg sl "$SL" '[$sl]')" \ --prohibit-public-ip-on-vnic false --wait-for-state AVAILABLE --query data.id --raw-output) oci iam availability-domain list -c "$T" --query 'data[].name' Choose an availability domain from that list. If OCI reports Out of host capacity , try another domain with the same subnet. You can also select VM.Standard.E5.Flex and repeat the image lookup to select the x86 image. AD='your availability domain name' SHAPE=VM.Standard.A1.Flex IMAGE=$(oci compute image list -c "$T" --shape "$SHAPE" \ --operating-system "Oracle Linux" --operating-system-version 9 \ --sort-by TIMECREATED --sort-order DESC --limit 1 --query 'data[0].id' --raw-output) VM=$(oci compute instance launch -c "$C" --availability-domain "$AD" \ --shape "$SHAPE" --shape-config '{"ocpus":2,"memoryInGBs":8}' --image-id "$IMAGE" \ --subnet-id "$SUBNET" --assign-public-ip true --display-name "$NAME-vm" \ --ssh-authorized-keys-file ssh_ed25519.pub --query data.id --raw-output) oci compute instance get --instance-id "$VM" --query 'data."lifecycle-state"' --raw-output Once the instance is RUNNING , retrieve its public IP and sign in. VM_IP=$(oci compute instance list-vnics --instance-id "$VM" \ --query 'data[0]."public-ip"' --raw-output) ssh -i ssh_ed25519 "opc@$VM_IP"

title: Installation
heading: Configure firewalld and install k3s
text: Run these commands on the VM. Keep TCP 6443 closed in the OCI security list. Local tools will reach the API through an SSH tunnel. The trusted sources below are the default pod and service CIDRs. K3s firewall requirements · K3s quick start sudo firewall-cmd --state sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=http sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=https sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-port=6443/tcp sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=trusted --add-source=10.42.0.0/16 sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=trusted --add-source=10.43.0.0/16 sudo firewall-cmd --reload curl -sfL https://get.k3s.io | sudo sh - sudo /usr/local/bin/k3s kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready node --all --timeout=180s sudo /usr/local/bin/k3s kubectl wait --for=create deployment/traefik -n kube-system --timeout=180s sudo /usr/local/bin/k3s kubectl rollout status deployment/traefik -n kube-system --timeout=180s

title: Installation
heading: Connect kubectl and Helm from your workstation
text: Install kubectl and Helm on your workstation. On macOS with Homebrew, use brew install kubectl helm . Install kubectl · Install Helm Return to the workstation shell in infrayard-host . The copied kubeconfig grants cluster-admin access. Keep it private and leave the server address at https://127.0.0.1:6443 for this tunnel. umask 077 ssh -i ssh_ed25519 "opc@$VM_IP" 'sudo cat /etc/rancher/k3s/k3s.yaml' > kubeconfig chmod 600 kubeconfig ssh -i ssh_ed25519 -fN -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes \ -L 127.0.0.1:6443:127.0.0.1:6443 "opc@$VM_IP" export KUBECONFIG="$PWD/kubeconfig" kubectl get nodes helm version --short Keep the tunnel running and return to the directory containing your OCI API key, such as infrayard-oci . Continue with the Kubernetes installation using storage class local-path . For a public portal, use the VM's public IP for DNS. A temporary evaluation can use a name such as 203-0-113-10.sslip.io with the octets of the VM's public IP. Verify that the name resolves before you request the certificate. Install on Kubernetes

title: Prepare OCI
heading: Overview
text: Infrayard creates OKE clusters with Terraform under one OCI user. This page creates that user, its permissions, an API key, the Terraform state bucket and the S3 key for the bucket. Every installation path needs these steps. Plan about 20 minutes in the OCI Console, or use the OCI CLI variant below. You need a user with administrator rights in the tenancy for these steps; Infrayard itself never gets them. At the end you have the values from the checklist .

title: Prepare OCI
heading: 1. Choose the anchor compartment
text: Infrayard creates everything it manages under one compartment , the anchor. By default each cluster gets its own child compartment with its network and node pools; a cluster can also use an existing compartment inside the anchor. Create a dedicated compartment, for example infrayard , or choose an existing one. Note its OCID (Identity & Security → Compartments → your compartment). Note its name path , which the policies use. For a nested compartment, write it with colons, for example platform:infrayard . Administrators can switch the anchor and region later in Admin → Configuration . The OCI user can only manage what the policies below allow.

title: Prepare OCI
heading: 2. Create the user and group
text: In Identity & Security → Domains → Default domain : Groups → Create group , name InfrayardServiceGroup . Users → Create user : first name Infrayard , last name Service , username infrayard-svc . An e-mail address is required; use a team mailbox. Clear Use the email address as the username . Open the user, Groups → Assign user to groups , select InfrayardServiceGroup . Copy the user OCID from the user's page. The user does not need a console password.

title: Prepare OCI
heading: 3. Add the policies
text: Identity & Security → Policies , select the root compartment , then Create policy . Name it infrayard-service , open the manual editor and paste the statements. Replace infrayard with your compartment name path. Allow group InfrayardServiceGroup to manage cluster-family in compartment infrayard Allow group InfrayardServiceGroup to manage virtual-network-family in compartment infrayard Allow group InfrayardServiceGroup to manage instance-family in compartment infrayard Allow group InfrayardServiceGroup to manage compartments in compartment infrayard Allow group InfrayardServiceGroup to manage object-family in compartment infrayard Allow group InfrayardServiceGroup to read all-resources in tenancy Allow group InfrayardServiceGroup to read tenancies in tenancy Allow group InfrayardServiceGroup to inspect compartments in tenancy Allow group InfrayardServiceGroup to use tag-namespaces in tenancy Allow service OKE to manage all-resources in tenancy What each part is for: Statements Why cluster-family , virtual-network-family , instance-family Create, scale, upgrade and delete OKE clusters, their VCNs and worker nodes compartments Create one child compartment per cluster and remove it on destroy object-family Read and write Terraform state in the bucket from step 5 read all-resources , read tenancies , inspect compartments List regions, shapes, Kubernetes versions, images and existing networks use tag-namespaces Required when your tenancy applies tag defaults to new resources. Infrayard itself sets free-form tags Allow service OKE … Lets the OKE service itself work in the tenancy. Keep it in this policy even if another policy already has it; a duplicate statement does no harm If the group lives in a domain other than Default , write it as group 'MyDomain'/'InfrayardServiceGroup' . Keep existing VCNs and subnets that clusters should use inside the anchor compartment; the policies above then cover them.

title: Prepare OCI
heading: 4. Create the API key
text: Open the infrayard-svc user → API keys → Add API key . Select Generate API key pair , click Download private key and save it as oci_api_key.pem . Click Add . The configuration preview shows user , fingerprint , tenancy and region . Note all four. The private key is the most sensitive item of the installation. Store it in your secret manager and do not e-mail it.

title: Prepare OCI
heading: 5. Create the Terraform state bucket
text: Storage → Object Storage → Buckets , select the anchor compartment , then Create bucket . Name: infrayard-tfstate . Keep the default Standard tier and enable Object versioning . Versioning keeps earlier state versions if something goes wrong. Note the namespace shown on the bucket page (also: oci os ns get ). Use a separate bucket for every Infrayard installation, for example for a test and a production portal. Infrayard stores each cluster's state as <user name>/<cluster name>.tfstate , so two installations that share a bucket can overwrite each other's state. Use the same region as the one in the API key preview.

title: Prepare OCI
heading: 6. Create the S3 key for the bucket
text: Terraform reaches the bucket through the S3-compatible API, which needs its own key. Open the infrayard-svc user → Customer secret keys → Generate secret key , name infrayard-tfstate . Copy the secret key right away. OCI shows it only once. Copy the access key from the list.

title: Prepare OCI
heading: The same steps with the OCI CLI
text: Instead of the Console you can run steps 1–6 with the OCI CLI, signed in as a tenancy administrator. The commands were tested in this order; they keep the generated values in shell variables and write the key files to the current directory. Run them in an empty directory that only you can read ( mkdir -m 700 infrayard-oci && cd infrayard-oci ). # Your tenancy OCID, as in ~/.oci/config of the administrator T=ocid1.tenancy.oc1..aaaa… # 1. Anchor compartment (skip and set C=<ocid> to use an existing one) C=$(oci iam compartment create -c $T --name infrayard \ --description "Infrayard anchor compartment" \ --wait-for-state ACTIVE --query data.id --raw-output) # 2. Group and user, user in the group G=$(oci iam group create -c $T --name InfrayardServiceGroup \ --description "Infrayard service user" --query data.id --raw-output) U=$(oci iam user create -c $T --name infrayard-svc \ --description "Infrayard service user" --email platform-team@example.com \ --query data.id --raw-output) oci iam group add-user --group-id $G --user-id $U # 3. Policy: save the ten statements from step 3 as a JSON list in policy.json, # one string per statement: ["Allow group …", "Allow group …", …] oci iam policy create -c $T --name infrayard-service \ --description "Infrayard service user" --statements file://policy.json # 4. API key: generate it locally and upload the public part umask 077 openssl genrsa -out oci_api_key.pem 2048 openssl rsa -pubout -in oci_api_key.pem -out oci_api_key_public.pem FP=$(oci iam user api-key upload --user-id $U \ --key-file oci_api_key_public.pem --query data.fingerprint --raw-output) # 5. State bucket with versioning, and the namespace oci os bucket create -c $C --name infrayard-tfstate --versioning Enabled NS=$(oci os ns get --query data --raw-output) # 6. S3 key: "id" is the access key, "key" the secret key (shown only once) oci iam customer-secret-key create --user-id $U --display-name infrayard-tfstate \ --query 'data.{access_key:id,secret_key:key}' --output json > s3-key.json echo "tenancy=$T user=$U fingerprint=$FP compartment=$C namespace=$NS" The last line prints the values for the checklist ; the S3 key pair is in s3-key.json . Store oci_api_key.pem and s3-key.json in your secret manager and delete the local copies after the installation.

title: Prepare OCI
heading: Check the setup
text: A new user and API key take a few minutes to work in every OCI service. During that time some calls fail with 401 NotAuthenticated even though everything is set up correctly; in our tests Identity accepted the key first, Container Engine and Object Storage about two minutes later. Wait five minutes before you start the installation or before you look for a mistake. To check the new user from your workstation, write a CLI configuration file for it (values from the checklist ): # infrayard-oci-config [DEFAULT] user=ocid1.user.oc1..aaaa… fingerprint=12:34:56:… tenancy=ocid1.tenancy.oc1..aaaa… region=eu-frankfurt-1 key_file=/full/path/to/oci_api_key.pem These three commands must succeed. They print the compartment name, a list of Kubernetes versions, and an empty list for the new bucket: oci --config-file infrayard-oci-config iam compartment get \ --compartment-id <anchor-compartment-ocid> --query data.name --raw-output oci --config-file infrayard-oci-config ce cluster-options get \ --cluster-option-id all --query 'data."kubernetes-versions"' oci --config-file infrayard-oci-config os object list --bucket-name infrayard-tfstate NotAuthorizedOrNotFound (404) instead means a policy is missing or names the wrong group or compartment. Infrayard runs the same kind of calls when an administrator syncs shapes and versions in Admin → Configuration .

title: Prepare OCI
heading: Values checklist
text: Value Example Where it comes from Tenancy OCID ocid1.tenancy.oc1..aaaa… API key preview User OCID ocid1.user.oc1..aaaa… Step 2 Fingerprint 12:34:56:… API key preview Region eu-frankfurt-1 API key preview Private key file oci_api_key.pem Step 4 Anchor compartment OCID ocid1.compartment.oc1..aaaa… Step 1 Object Storage namespace frxyz1abcd Step 5 State bucket infrayard-tfstate Step 5 S3 access key and secret key 0a1b2c… Step 6 Continue with Install on Kubernetes .

title: Install on Kubernetes
heading: Overview
text: This guide installs Infrayard with Helm into a Kubernetes cluster you already run: an OKE cluster, k3s or another distribution. The steps are the same everywhere; where OKE and k3s differ, both variants are shown. Infrayard is tested with this guide on OKE (Kubernetes 1.36, one VM.Standard.E4.Flex worker with 1 OCPU and 8 GB) and on k3s, both with Traefik and cert-manager. Time needed: about 30 minutes, after Prepare OCI .

title: Install on Kubernetes
heading: What you need
text: A Kubernetes cluster and kubectl access. Step 1 installs cluster-wide resources (cert-manager and its CRDs, the Let's Encrypt issuer) and needs cluster-admin rights; the Infrayard chart itself creates only namespaced resources. Helm 3.8 or newer on your workstation. An ingress controller. OKE has none by default; k3s ships Traefik. cert-manager for Let's Encrypt certificates, or your own TLS certificate. A StorageClass for the PostgreSQL volume. The chart requests 10 GiB. OKE: oci-bv , which creates a 50 GB block volume, the OCI minimum. k3s: local-path . Free capacity of about 1 CPU and 2 GiB memory. Limits allow peaks up to 3.7 CPU and 3.2 GiB. Outbound internet access from the pods. Each cluster deployment downloads the Terraform providers from registry.terraform.io , releases.hashicorp.com and GitHub releases. On OKE with private worker nodes, this traffic goes through the VCN's NAT gateway; a service gateway alone is not enough. A DNS name for the portal, for example infrayard.example.com . Keycloak is served on the same name under /auth , so one name is enough. The values from the OCI checklist . The registry user, token, address and Infrayard version from your onboarding e-mail. Step 2 uses 1.0.0 as an example. The examples use the namespace infrayard , the release name infrayard and the registry registry.gitlab.com/solvialab/infrayard . Use the registry address and version from your onboarding e-mail.

title: Install on Kubernetes
heading: 1. Ingress controller and certificates
text: Reuse your ingress controller and cert-manager if they are already installed. For automatic TLS, configure or reuse a ClusterIssuer and use its name in step 4. OKE: Install Traefik if you need an ingress controller. The chart creates an OCI flexible load balancer with a public IP. helm repo add traefik https://traefik.github.io/charts helm install traefik traefik/traefik -n traefik --create-namespace \ --set-string service.annotations."service\.beta\.kubernetes\.io/oci-load-balancer-shape"=flexible \ --set-string service.annotations."service\.beta\.kubernetes\.io/oci-load-balancer-shape-flex-min"=10 \ --set-string service.annotations."service\.beta\.kubernetes\.io/oci-load-balancer-shape-flex-max"=100 Use --set-string : annotations must be strings, and with --set Helm reads 10 and 100 as numbers and the install fails. The load balancer gets its public IP within about a minute; kubectl get svc -n traefik traefik shows it as EXTERNAL-IP . The load balancer subnet must allow TCP 80 and 443 from the internet in its security list or network security group: 80 for Let's Encrypt, 443 for users. Clusters created by Infrayard have these rules. OKE opens the node ports from the load balancer to the worker nodes on its own. For a portal reachable only from your VPN, use an internal load balancer instead; see private access . k3s: Traefik is already running in kube-system . Install cert-manager on OKE or k3s if it is missing from your cluster. helm repo add jetstack https://charts.jetstack.io helm install cert-manager jetstack/cert-manager -n cert-manager --create-namespace \ --set crds.enabled=true Then create a Let's Encrypt issuer. It needs no e-mail address; Let's Encrypt no longer sends expiry e-mails, and cert-manager renews the certificate on its own: kubectl apply -f - <<'EOF' apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1 kind: ClusterIssuer metadata: name: letsencrypt spec: acme: server: https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory privateKeySecretRef: name: letsencrypt solvers: - http01: ingress: ingressClassName: traefik EOF kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready clusterissuer/letsencrypt --timeout=120s Let's Encrypt must reach the portal on port 80 from the internet. If it cannot, use your own certificate (step 4).

title: Install on Kubernetes
heading: 2. Log in to the registry
text: The chart and the images are in the same private registry. Use the same Bash shell for the remaining steps so they can read the variables you set here. When prompted, enter the registry credentials from your onboarding e-mail. VERSION=1.0.0 # Replace with the version from your onboarding e-mail. read -r -p 'Registry user: ' REGISTRY_USER read -rs -p 'Registry token: ' REGISTRY_TOKEN printf '\n' printf '%s' "$REGISTRY_TOKEN" | helm registry login registry.gitlab.com -u "$REGISTRY_USER" --password-stdin Check that you can read the chart. helm show chart oci://registry.gitlab.com/solvialab/infrayard/charts/infrayard --version "$VERSION" Check that both version and appVersion match VERSION . If you get 401 , 403 or denied , check your login and the token's registry access. Troubleshooting

title: Install on Kubernetes
heading: 3. Create the namespace and secrets
text: Create two Kubernetes Secrets outside Helm. This block uses jq and the registry credentials from step 2. Run it from the directory containing oci_api_key.pem . kubectl create namespace infrayard # Lets Kubernetes pull the images printf '%s' "$REGISTRY_TOKEN" | jq -cRs --arg user "$REGISTRY_USER" \ '{auths:{"registry.gitlab.com":{auth:(($user + ":" + .)|@base64)}}}' | kubectl create secret generic regcred -n infrayard \ --type=kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson --from-file=.dockerconfigjson=/dev/stdin unset REGISTRY_TOKEN # OCI API private key of the infrayard-svc user kubectl create secret generic infrayard-oci-key -n infrayard \ --from-file=oci_api_key.pem=./oci_api_key.pem The key name inside the secret must be oci_api_key.pem . Without this secret the API pod stays in Init or ContainerCreating .

title: Install on Kubernetes
heading: 4. Write the values files
text: Keep settings and passwords in two files. values.yaml can go into your configuration repository; secrets.yaml belongs in your secret manager. values.yaml : global: domain: infrayard.example.com imagePullSecrets: - name: regcred api: image: repository: registry.gitlab.com/solvialab/infrayard/api oci: tenancyOcid: ocid1.tenancy.oc1..aaaa... userOcid: ocid1.user.oc1..aaaa... fingerprint: "12:34:56:78:90:ab:cd:ef:12:34:56:78:90:ab:cd:ef" region: eu-frankfurt-1 namespace: frxyz1abcd parentCompartmentOcid: ocid1.compartment.oc1..aaaa... terraform: stateBucket: infrayard-tfstate frontend: image: repository: registry.gitlab.com/solvialab/infrayard/frontend postgresql: storage: storageClass: oci-bv # OKE. k3s: local-path. Empty: cluster default keycloak: realmImport: initialAdmin: # first Infrayard administrator username: admin email: admin@example.com ingress: className: traefik # or nginx, or your controller's class annotations: cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt tls: enabled: true secretName: infrayard-tls secrets.yaml . Generate each of the three passwords with openssl rand -hex 24 ; hex passwords contain no characters that need escaping: postgresql: auth: password: "<database password>" keycloak: admin: password: "<Keycloak master admin password>" realmImport: initialAdmin: password: "<temporary password of the first admin>" api: terraform: s3AccessKey: "<S3 access key>" s3SecretKey: "<S3 secret key>" chmod 600 secrets.yaml Notes: Own certificate instead of Let's Encrypt: create the secret with kubectl create secret tls infrayard-tls -n infrayard --cert=fullchain.pem --key=privkey.pem and remove the cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer annotation. ingress-nginx: set className: nginx and add the annotations nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout: "3600" and nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-buffering: "off" , so that live Terraform logs are not cut off. Your own Keycloak instead of the bundled one: see Use your own Keycloak before installing. E-mail notifications (optional): set api.email.enabled: true , api.email.adminEmails and the api.email.smtp block, with the SMTP password in secrets.yaml . Test or demo installation: frontend.robots.noindex: true asks search engines not to index the portal. Single-node clusters: the chart tolerates the control-plane taint by default, so all pods can run on one k3s node.

title: Install on Kubernetes
heading: 5. Install
text: helm install infrayard oci://registry.gitlab.com/solvialab/infrayard/charts/infrayard \ --version "$VERSION" -n infrayard -f values.yaml -f secrets.yaml The chart version selects the matching image version automatically; do not set an image tag. Watch the pods until all four are Running and ready, usually within two minutes. Keycloak is the last one, because it imports the realm on the first start: kubectl get pods -n infrayard -w NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE infrayard-api-6c9f7d8b5-x2kqp 1/1 Running 0 2m infrayard-frontend-5bd8c7f9d4-7wq9z 1/1 Running 0 2m infrayard-keycloak-7d9b6f5c8-k4m2n 1/1 Running 0 2m infrayard-postgresql-0 1/1 Running 0 2m

title: Install on Kubernetes
heading: 6. Point DNS to the cluster
text: Find the external IP of the ingress controller: kubectl get svc -n traefik traefik # OKE with Traefik from step 1 kubectl get svc -n kube-system traefik # k3s If you use your own domain on OKE, point its A record to the EXTERNAL-IP . k3s on a cloud VM (for example OCI Compute): k3s publishes Traefik on the node's own address, so EXTERNAL-IP shows the VM's private IP, such as 10.0.0.12 . Point DNS to the VM's public IP instead, and allow TCP 80 and 443 in the VM's security list or network security group and in the host firewall. For a VPN-only portal, use the private IP; see private access . For a temporary k3s evaluation using sslip.io , use the same name as global.domain in step 4. That name supplies its own A record. Run dig +short "$PORTAL_DOMAIN" A with PORTAL_DOMAIN set to the name and check that it returns the VM's public IP. Once DNS resolves, cert-manager obtains the certificate, usually within two minutes: kubectl get certificate -n infrayard # NAME READY SECRET AGE # infrayard-tls True infrayard-tls 2m

title: Install on Kubernetes
heading: 7. Sign in
text: Open https://infrayard.example.com and sign in with the first admin's user name and temporary password. Keycloak asks for a new password right away. Then, in Admin → Configuration : Check the region and the anchor compartment. In Available Node Shapes , click Sync from OCI . In Available K8s Versions , click Refresh from OCI . Enable the shapes and versions your users may choose. New versions start disabled. Set Kubernetes API Access under OCI Settings . Infrayard calls the API of every new cluster on port 6443 to issue kubeconfigs, so it needs a network path to it. With the box off (the default), clusters get a private endpoint. Infrayard creates a new VCN for each cluster unless you supply one, so it reaches a private endpoint only if its own network is routed into that VCN; without such a route the cluster still deploys, but the kubeconfig download fails. To use a public endpoint instead, turn on Public endpoint restricted by CIDR allowlist , enter your VPN or office ranges and Infrayard's own outbound address in Allowed API CIDRs , and click Save OCI settings . On OKE with private worker nodes, that address is the public IP of the NAT gateway in the VCN of the cluster that runs Infrayard: oci network nat-gateway list -c <compartment of that VCN> --query 'data[]."nat-ip"' On a k3s VM with a public IP, it is that IP. The setting applies to clusters created afterwards. Review the default limits and the templates. Create a small test cluster and watch the Terraform log. It ends with OK Cluster ready for kubeconfig downloads ; if it reports Cluster API endpoint … not reachable from Infrayard instead, fix the API access from step 3. When the cluster reaches Running , download the kubeconfig and run kubectl get nodes . Destroy the test cluster afterwards. This run proves the OCI policies, the state bucket and the network path to the cluster API; a successful helm install alone does not. See cluster lifecycle .

title: Install on Kubernetes
heading: Add users
text: With the bundled Keycloak, users are managed in the Keycloak admin console, which is not exposed on the internet. Open it through a port forward: kubectl port-forward -n infrayard svc/infrayard-keycloak 8080:8080 Go to http://localhost:8080/auth/admin and sign in as admin with the Keycloak master admin password from step 4. Open Manage realms and select infrayard . In Users → Add user , fill in the user details and click Create . Open Credentials → Set password , keep Temporary on, click Save , and confirm with Save password . The user sets a new password at first sign-in. For an administrator: Role mapping → Assign role → admin . Users without the admin role can sign in, deploy clusters within their limits and see the templates allowed for their roles. To connect Infrayard to your company Keycloak instead, see Use your own Keycloak .

title: Install on Kubernetes
heading: Reference: all settings
text: helm show values oci://registry.gitlab.com/solvialab/infrayard/charts/infrayard --version "$VERSION" Every value is documented in that output. After the installation, helm status infrayard -n infrayard prints the portal URL and the sign-in summary again. Next: restrict access to your VPN and plan upgrades and backups .

title: Use your own Keycloak
heading: Overview
text: By default Infrayard brings its own Keycloak with a ready realm. If your company already runs Keycloak, Infrayard can sign users in through a realm there instead, so people use their existing accounts and you manage access with roles or groups you already have. This option is available for the Kubernetes installation . It is tested with Keycloak 22 and 26; use Keycloak 22 or newer.

title: Use your own Keycloak
heading: How sign-in works
text: The portal sends the user to your Keycloak login page (OpenID Connect, Authorization Code flow with PKCE). Keycloak returns an access token to the portal client infrayard-portal . It is a public client: there is no client secret to store. The Infrayard API checks the token's signature against the realm keys, its issuer and that it was issued to infrayard-portal . On the first sign-in Infrayard creates its own user record from the token. There is no directory sync. The token must contain sub , preferred_username , email and the roles or groups described below. Keycloak includes them by default.

title: Use your own Keycloak
heading: Roles
text: Role Default name What it does Admin role admin Administration: all clusters, users, configuration, templates, requests and audit log Access role none When set, only users with this role (or the admin role) may use Infrayard. Others see "Your account is not allowed to use Infrayard" and are signed out Template roles your choice, for example testing , production Templates can require a role; only users holding it see the template In a shared company realm, choose names that cannot clash with existing roles, such as infrayard-admin and infrayard-user , and always set the access role. Without it, every account in the realm can sign in and create clusters within the default limits. Infrayard can read these names from one of three places in the token: Source rolesClaim value You assign Realm roles (default) realm_access.roles Realm roles, directly or through a group Client roles resource_access.infrayard-portal.roles Roles of the client infrayard-portal Groups groups Group membership (the group name is compared)

title: Use your own Keycloak
heading: 1. Set the Helm values
text: Add these values to your values.yaml from the Kubernetes guide : keycloak: enabled: false # do not install the bundled Keycloak api: oidc: issuer: https://sso.example.com/realms/acme clientId: infrayard-portal rolesClaim: realm_access.roles adminRole: infrayard-admin requiredRole: infrayard-user The issuer must be exactly the iss value of your tokens. Check it at https://sso.example.com/realms/acme/.well-known/openid-configuration . Keycloak versions before 17, and some installations, use the path /auth/realms/acme . The keycloak.admin.password and keycloak.realmImport values are not needed in this mode.

title: Use your own Keycloak
heading: 2. Install and import the client
text: Install or upgrade with Helm as in the Kubernetes guide. The chart then prepares a Keycloak import file that matches your values: the client, the admin and access roles, and for rolesClaim: groups the groups and the group mapper. Export it: kubectl get configmap infrayard-oidc-client -n infrayard \ -o jsonpath='{.data.keycloak-partial-import\.json}' > infrayard-keycloak.json In the Keycloak admin console, open your realm, then Realm settings → Action (top right) → Partial import . Select the file, choose If a resource exists: Skip and click Import . The imported client infrayard-portal is public, uses the Standard flow with PKCE (S256) and allows https://infrayard.example.com/* as redirect and post-logout URL. helm status infrayard -n infrayard prints the same instructions with your values.

title: Use your own Keycloak
heading: 3. Give users access
text: Assign the admin role and the access role to the right people, preferably through groups. For example, in Groups → platform-team → Role mapping → Assign role , add infrayard-admin ; in Groups → engineering , add infrayard-user . Sign in at https://infrayard.example.com with an admin account and open Admin . A role change takes effect with the user's next token, at the latest after the access token lifetime of your realm (5 minutes by default). Users whose role was removed are signed out with a message; users whose Keycloak session ends are signed out as well.

title: Use your own Keycloak
heading: Keycloak with a private CA
text: If Keycloak's certificate comes from an internal company CA, browsers trust it through your device management, but the Infrayard API needs the CA explicitly to fetch the realm keys. Add the CA certificate: api: oidc: ca: cert: | -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE----- MIIDdzCCAl+gAwIBAgIU... -----END CERTIFICATE----- Or reference an existing ConfigMap in the infrayard namespace, for example one managed by trust-manager: api: oidc: ca: existingConfigMap: company-ca key: ca.crt Public CAs remain trusted in both cases.

title: Use your own Keycloak
heading: Keycloak under another address inside the cluster
text: Users reach Keycloak at the public issuer address. If the Infrayard API cannot use that address (split-horizon DNS, no route from the cluster to it), give it an internal address of the same realm: api: oidc: issuer: https://sso.example.com/realms/acme internalUrl: http://keycloak.sso.svc.cluster.local:8080/realms/acme Only the signing keys are fetched there; tokens must still carry the public issuer.

title: Use your own Keycloak
heading: Changing the role source later
text: The import uses Skip for existing objects. If you later switch to rolesClaim: groups , the existing client does not get the group mapper. Add a Group membership mapper named groups (token claim name groups , full group path off) to the client's dedicated scope, or delete the client and import the new file.

title: Use your own Keycloak
heading: Troubleshooting
text: Symptom Cause and fix After the Keycloak login the portal does not load your data (API answers 401) issuer differs from the token's iss (for example /auth in the path). Compare with the realm's .well-known/openid-configuration "Your account is not allowed to use Infrayard" The user lacks the access role, or rolesClaim points to the wrong place. Decode a token and check the claim No Admin menu for an admin The admin role is not in the claim named by rolesClaim API log: Cannot fetch OIDC signing keys The API cannot reach Keycloak or does not trust its certificate. Set internalUrl or ca Keycloak error "Invalid parameter: redirect_uri" The client's redirect URI does not match the Infrayard domain. Re-import, or fix the client's Valid redirect URIs

title: Private access (VPN only)
heading: Overview
text: Infrayard holds credentials that can create and delete infrastructure in your OCI tenancy. We strongly recommend that the portal is reachable only from your company network or VPN, not from the whole internet. Infrayard does not restrict network access by itself: this is part of your network setup, and this page shows the usual ways to do it. Keep in mind what still has to work: Inbound: users on the VPN reach the portal on port 443. With the bundled Keycloak, sign-in runs on the same address under /auth , so it becomes private too. Outbound from Infrayard: OCI APIs, the image registry, and the Kubernetes API (port 6443) of every cluster it creates. A NAT gateway or your proxy path is enough; Infrayard needs no inbound connection from the internet. Clusters: users need a route from the VPN to the Kubernetes API of their clusters to use kubectl . See Kubernetes API access .

title: Private access (VPN only)
heading: Option A: private address (recommended)
text: The portal gets an IP address inside your VCN and has no public IP at all. The VPN reaches the VCN through a dynamic routing gateway (Site-to-Site VPN or FastConnect) or through a VPN server in the VCN. OKE with Traefik: install Traefik with an internal load balancer in a private subnet. OCI does not change an existing load balancer from public to private: if Traefik already runs with a public one, remove it first with helm uninstall traefik -n traefik . The new load balancer receives a private IP. helm install traefik traefik/traefik -n traefik --create-namespace \ --set-string service.annotations."service\.beta\.kubernetes\.io/oci-load-balancer-internal"=true \ --set-string service.annotations."service\.beta\.kubernetes\.io/oci-load-balancer-subnet1"=<private-subnet-ocid> \ --set-string service.annotations."service\.beta\.kubernetes\.io/oci-load-balancer-shape"=flexible \ --set-string service.annotations."service\.beta\.kubernetes\.io/oci-load-balancer-shape-flex-min"=10 \ --set-string service.annotations."service\.beta\.kubernetes\.io/oci-load-balancer-shape-flex-max"=100 Annotations must be strings; with --set , Helm reads true and the numbers as other types and the install fails. Other Kubernetes distributions: use your platform's internal load balancer, or expose the ingress controller only on the nodes' private addresses. k3s on a single VM: create the VM in a private subnet without a public IP. Give the subnet a NAT gateway for outbound traffic.

title: Private access (VPN only)
heading: Option B: public address with an allowlist
text: The portal keeps its public IP, but only your VPN's egress addresses may connect. In OCI, add an ingress rule for TCP 443 (and 80) from your VPN CIDR ranges only, in the network security group or security list of the load balancer or the VM, and remove any rule that allows 0.0.0.0/0 . This is quicker to set up but depends on the VPN's public addresses staying the same.

title: Private access (VPN only)
heading: Certificates for a private portal
text: Let's Encrypt's standard check (HTTP-01) connects to your portal from the internet, so it fails once the portal is private. Choose one of these: Certificate How From your company CA kubectl create secret tls infrayard-tls -n infrayard --cert=fullchain.pem --key=privkey.pem and remove the cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer annotation from the values Let's Encrypt with a DNS check (DNS-01) A cert-manager ClusterIssuer with a DNS-01 solver for your DNS provider A company CA certificate must be trusted on users' devices; for a public DNS-01 certificate nothing extra is needed. Renew company CA certificates before they expire: Infrayard does not do that for you.

title: Private access (VPN only)
heading: DNS
text: Point infrayard.example.com to the private IP in your internal DNS, for example a private view in OCI DNS or your company DNS that VPN clients use. A public DNS record with a private IP also works, but it publishes the internal address.

title: Private access (VPN only)
heading: Your own Keycloak
text: If you use your own Keycloak , users' browsers must reach it from the VPN, and the Infrayard API must reach it from the cluster. If the API sees Keycloak under a different internal address, set api.oidc.internalUrl .

title: Private access (VPN only)
heading: Cluster API endpoints
text: Clusters created by Infrayard can use a private Kubernetes API endpoint or a public one restricted to allowed source ranges. With a restricted public endpoint, add the VPN's egress ranges and Infrayard's own outbound address to Allowed API CIDRs in Admin → Configuration → OCI Settings ; Infrayard calls the cluster API to issue kubeconfigs. See networking .

title: Private access (VPN only)
heading: Check it
text: From a machine outside the VPN, the portal must not answer: curl -m 10 -sS -o /dev/null https://infrayard.example.com && echo "STILL PUBLIC" From the VPN, it must load and sign-in must work. Then create a test cluster and download its kubeconfig to confirm that Infrayard still reaches OCI and the cluster API.

title: Cluster lifecycle
heading: Overview
text: These workflows apply to supported OKE clusters managed through Infrayard. Check your cluster tier and network prerequisites before making changes.

title: Cluster lifecycle
heading: Signing in
text: Infrayard signs you in through Keycloak — the bundled instance or your organisation's existing Keycloak. Click Log In — you are redirected to the Keycloak login page and returned to the portal after authentication. No separate Infrayard account is needed.

title: Cluster lifecycle
heading: Deploying a cluster
text: Navigate to Deploy from the top nav (Optional) Select a Cluster template — pre-configured profiles created by your admin that pre-fill and lock resource fields (pools, nodes, CPU, RAM, storage). Choose "Custom" to configure everything manually with your account's limits enforced Enter a Cluster name — this becomes the base name for all OCI resources ( {name}-cluster , {name}-vcn , etc.) Choose a CIDR range from the available pool — each cluster gets its own /24 Select a Kubernetes version , VM shape , and Node image (locked if the template defines them; otherwise user-selectable — image defaults to auto-select if none configured) If using "Custom" mode, configure one or more Node pools — each pool has a name, node count, OCPU, RAM, and storage, constrained by your account's effective limits (Optional) Use the Advanced tab to bring existing OCI infrastructure — your own VCN, compartment, or subnet Review the Deployment Summary — shows all resources that will be created, plus live estimated monthly and hourly cost Click Deploy Infrayard runs terraform apply and streams the live output in the portal. The cluster appears in My Clusters once provisioning completes. The deploy form enforces your account's effective limits — maximum pools, nodes, OCPU, RAM, and storage. If a limit prevents you from deploying, submit a limit-increase request from the deploy or scale flow; admins can approve granted values into your per-user overrides.

title: Cluster lifecycle
heading: Scaling a cluster
text: In My Clusters , click Scale on a running cluster Adjust resources per pool — nodes, OCPU, RAM, and storage Add new node pools or remove existing ones as needed; new pools default their name to the cluster's bare name and accept any name that matches the standard pool-name rules (lowercase, alphanumeric + hyphen, 32 chars max). Existing pool names stay immutable to keep Terraform/OKE state aligned. Review the change preview and click Apply Scaling behaviour depends on the cluster tier configured by your admin — see Cluster tiers . Kubernetes version changes are handled via a separate Upgrade action.

title: Cluster lifecycle
heading: Destroying a cluster
text: In My Clusters , click Destroy Infrayard runs terraform plan -destroy and shows the exact resources that will be removed Confirm — terraform destroy runs and cluster-scoped OCI resources are cleaned up The CIDR range is returned to the pool and available for reuse Destroy is permanent and cannot be undone. Requests workflow: The admin Requests area handles both protected-cluster destroy approvals and per-user limit-increase requests. Users submit a reason instead of destroying directly or when they need higher limits; admins approve, adjust, or deny with a note. Destroy approval still opens the Terraform destroy plan before force-destroy. Limit approval writes granted values into the user's per-user overrides. Results appear in the user's Activity inbox, and SMTP-enabled installs can also send info-only email pings with requester, action, comments, and request parameters. Destroy behavior note: Infrayard-managed child compartments may be deleted with the cluster. External compartment overrides are retained for shared/multi-cluster setups. In Object Storage, only the destroyed cluster's .tfstate object is removed; the user-level prefix/folder is kept for other clusters.

title: Cluster lifecycle
heading: Activity
text: The user nav includes an Activity inbox with an unread badge. It persists important events across refreshes and sessions; today it records destroy-request approvals/denials, limit request submissions and reviews, TTL expiry warnings at 24h, 4h, and 1h remaining, deploy/scale/upgrade/destroy start and completion events, and admin-driven account limit changes. Administrators also receive the deploy, scale, upgrade and destroy events of other users' clusters, with the owner's name, and an entry for every new destroy or limit request.

title: Cluster lifecycle
heading: Cluster detail
text: Click Details on any cluster card to see: Cluster information — name, status, K8s version, region, CIDR, compartment, VM shape, cluster tier, estimated monthly cost, OCID Node pools — pool name, node count, OCPU, RAM, storage, and status per pool Cost breakdown — per-pool monthly cost, control plane cost (Enhanced tier), and total with hourly rate Access — kubeconfig download and SSH key download (see Kubernetes access )

title: Cluster lifecycle
heading: Cluster tiers
text: The admin configures which cluster tier(s) the platform allows: Basic only , Enhanced only , or Both . When a single tier is allowed, users see it as an informational indicator on the deploy form. When Both is allowed, the deploy form shows a tier picker so each user picks per cluster — useful when one team wants free/dev clusters and another wants production-grade scaling, all served by the same platform. Basic Enhanced Cost Free Oracle's current Enhanced control-plane rate Node scaling ⚠️ Full — add/remove nodes or pools is automatic; resource-profile changes require manual cycling ✅ Full in-place Cluster Autoscaler ❌ ✅ Best for Dev/test, cost-sensitive teams Production, automated scaling Basic cluster scaling: Both Basic and Enhanced clusters support full scaling — nodes, OCPU, RAM, and storage. In Basic clusters, adding/removing nodes or node pools is automatic and does not require manual rotation. Manual cycling is required when changing per-node resources (shape, OCPU, RAM, storage), and is also recommended after a Kubernetes upgrade so workers pick up the new target image/version. OKE → Cluster → Node Pool → Nodes → Cordon & drain → Terminate Recommended rolling cycle for each affected Basic node pool (current size = N ): Scale from N to 2N Wait until the additional N nodes are Ready/Active Scale back from 2N to N (OKE removes extra nodes automatically) Verify workloads and node health before moving to the next pool The portal shows tier-specific warnings/messages for this flow. Kubernetes version upgrades: Use Upgrade k8s on a running cluster. This updates the control plane and node-pool target Kubernetes/image configuration: Direct upgrades are limited to the same or next minor version (for example 1.33.x -> 1.34.x ; not 1.33.x -> 1.35.x ). Basic: perform rolling worker refresh per pool ( N -> 2N -> N ) after nodes become Ready/Active ; the Upgrade modal shows live per-pool steps based on current node counts. Enhanced: rollout is fully automated (control plane plus worker refresh), no manual cycling required. Switching tiers: Admins can switch the platform tier at any time in Configuration — Basic, Enhanced, or Both. The change applies to all new clusters; existing clusters retain the tier they were provisioned with. Per-user tier override: Admins can pin a specific user to Basic or to Enhanced, regardless of the global setting. The override is force-only (single tier per user); a user without an override inherits whatever the global setting allows, including the per-cluster picker when the global is Both .

title: Cluster lifecycle
heading: Kubernetes upgrades
text: Dedicated action — available from cluster detail and dashboard actions Shape-aware + allowlist-aware — upgrade options are filtered to OCI-compatible versions enabled by admin config Sequential minors only — direct upgrades allow same/next minor only; skip-minor upgrades are blocked with explicit error Control plane + node-pool target update — upgrade action updates cluster Kubernetes and node-pool target version/image Basic upgrade behavior — perform rolling worker refresh per pool ( N -> 2N -> N ) after new nodes are Ready/Active Enhanced upgrade behavior — fully automated rollout (control plane + workers), no manual cycling required Tier guidance in UI — Basic and Enhanced show upgrade-specific notes with rollout guidance Dynamic Basic rollout guidance — Basic upgrade modal reads live pool/node counts and renders exact per-pool steps (for example 1 -> 2 -> 1 or 3 -> 6 -> 3 ) instead of a static example

title: Cluster lifecycle
heading: Expiry and cleanup
text: A time-to-live can be set for temporary clusters. When its TTL is reached, Infrayard starts the destroy workflow. Use TTL deliberately and check how it interacts with your protected-cluster policy. Activity includes expiry warnings at 24 hours, 4 hours and 1 hour remaining. Scaling a Basic cluster to zero worker nodes can pause compute use, but does not guarantee a zero Oracle bill: retained resources and other services can still be charged. Review operating responsibilities before production changes.

title: Administration
heading: Overview
text: Administrators configure the approved options and operating boundaries available to each team. Review security and access for the identity and privilege model. Admin access is granted by the admin role in Keycloak ( admin in the bundled realm; with your own Keycloak a realm role, client role or group you choose, see roles ). Admins see an Admin panel in the top navigation.

title: Administration
heading: All clusters
text: A full view of every cluster across all users — status, owner, CIDR, K8s version, tier, resource counts, estimated cost (monthly + hourly), and age. The stats cards show online, provisioning, upgrading k8s, destroying, failed, total, CIDRs used, and monthly spend. From this view admins can: Click Details on any cluster to open its full detail view including kubeconfig and SSH key download Click Scale on Active/Error clusters to adjust pools, nodes, and per-node resources Click Upgrade k8s on Active/Error clusters to upgrade Kubernetes version Click Destroy to destroy any cluster regardless of owner Click View logs while an operation is running or after a failure Click New Cluster to provision a cluster outside of normal user quotas

title: Administration
heading: Users & limits
text: Lists every user who has signed into Infrayard. For each user, admins can: View current cluster count and active limit View resolved effective limits (per-user override if set, otherwise global default) Click Edit Limits to set per-user overrides for any combination of: cluster limit, pool max, node max, OCPU, RAM, storage, and cluster tier Reset a user's overrides back to global defaults; direct admin limit edits and resets create user Activity notifications Reset all overrides at once to revert the user to global platform defaults Limit changes take effect on the user's next page load or login — no restart required.

title: Administration
heading: Configuration
text: Platform-wide settings manageable at runtime — no redeployment needed: Setting Description Cluster tier Basic (free), Enhanced (Oracle's current Enhanced control-plane rate), or Both — applies to all new clusters; "Both" lets the user pick per cluster on the deploy form Cluster limit Default max active clusters per user Node pool limit Max pools per cluster Nodes per pool Max nodes per pool OCPU / RAM / Storage Max compute per node CIDR pool Add, remove, and enable/disable /24 ranges available for cluster allocation VM shapes Sync from OCI, plus add/remove/enable/disable shapes in the deploy form K8s versions Add, remove, and enable/disable Kubernetes versions Node images Add, remove, and enable/disable OCI compute images for worker node pools Note: Shape and image availability is region- and tenancy-specific. In Admin → Configuration , use Sync from OCI in the VM Shapes section first, then curate/label as needed. For CLI verification, fetch current OKE node pool options in the target region: oci ce node-pool-options get --node-pool-option-id all --profile <PROFILE> Use the returned shapes and sources lists as the source of truth for VM shapes and node images. If Sync from OCI is unavailable, Infrayard keeps existing shape config unchanged and you can continue with manual curation from the CLI output above. Sync uses the API pod OCI service account credentials/policies (not the browser/user profile). K8s version freshness: OCI can publish new OKE patch versions after Infrayard is deployed. The platform now auto-syncs available OKE versions in the background (default daily) so admin config stays current without anyone clicking Refresh from OCI . Newly-fetched versions land disabled by default — admins still curate which versions users may deploy. Refresh from OCI remains available for on-demand pulls (e.g. before template reviews or upgrade waves). Upgrade recommendation pills use the latest enabled version, so stale enablement can hide available upgrades. Once a cluster's K8s version falls behind the latest enabled, a separate sweeper (default hourly) emits one Activity entry plus one email to the cluster owner per (cluster, target version) pair, so the owner is told about new upgrade options even when not actively logged in. The notification is idempotent — it does not re-fire for the same target — and the marker auto-resets after the cluster is upgraded, ready to fire again on the next enabled-version bump. Deploy form behavior: Kubernetes versions are filtered by the currently selected VM shape and region. Users only see versions that are both OCI-compatible for that shape (based on OKE node image availability) and enabled in Admin Configuration. If compatibility lookup is unavailable, the K8s list is not shown (fail-closed) and deploy is blocked until validation succeeds. If a version is missing, either enable it in Admin Configuration or choose a shape that supports it.

title: Administration
heading: Cluster templates
text: Templates are administrator-approved configurations. Template-defined resource values can exceed a user's personal custom-deployment limits; the locked fields prevent the user from editing those pre-approved values. Review template scope and required roles accordingly. Dedicated admin page for creating and managing cluster templates — pre-configured profiles that appear as selectable cards on the deploy form. Templates encode: Setting Description K8s version Pre-selected Kubernetes version (optional — user selects if not set) VM shape Pre-selected node shape (optional) Node image Pre-selected OCI compute image (optional — auto-selects latest OKE image if not set) Node pools Pre-defined pool layout — name, node count, OCPU, RAM, storage per pool Tier default Suggested cluster tier — Basic or Enhanced (suggestion only, not enforced) TTL Optional time-to-live in hours — when reached, Infrayard automatically starts cluster destroy/cleanup Destroy protection When enabled, the "Destroy" button on the user's cluster opens a "Request destroy" modal instead. Requests land in Admin → Requests (with a live count badge in the nav) where an admin approves, reviews the destroy plan, then confirms force-destroy, or denies with a note Required role Keycloak role (or group, depending on your role source) — only users with it can see and use the template. Leave empty for all users Sort order Controls display position in the deploy form (lower numbers appear first) The templates table shows estimated monthly and hourly cost per template. The add/edit modal includes a live cost preview that updates as you change pools, shape, or tier. Template modal behavior: when a VM shape is selected, the K8s dropdown is filtered to versions OCI reports as compatible for that shape in the current region (node-image-backed compatibility). If compatibility lookup is unavailable, no fallback list is shown (fail-closed). Template save/update re-validates shape+K8s compatibility and blocks incompatible combinations. Environment-tier gating — use required_role to control which teams can deploy which cluster sizes. For example, create a DEV — Small template visible to everyone, a TEST — Medium template requiring a testing role, a UAT — Large template requiring a uat role, and a PROD — HA template requiring a production role. Users only see the templates they have access to on the deploy form. Create the roles in Keycloak under Realm roles (or as client roles or groups, matching your role source ) and assign them to the relevant users. Templates can be created, edited, enabled/disabled, and permanently deleted. Disabled templates no longer appear in the deploy form but remain referenced by existing clusters. Permanently deleting a template removes it from the admin panel entirely.

title: Administration
heading: Requests
text: Approval queue for user-submitted destroy requests on protection-enabled clusters and limit-increase requests for per-user overrides. The admin nav shows live request count badges that refresh every 5 seconds (hidden when zero pending). Filter by Pending / Approved / Denied / All. Each pending row has a Review action. When SMTP is configured, request submit/review events also send info-only email pings: admins get submit notifications, and users get submit/approve/deny notifications. For destroy requests, the review modal lets the admin: Add an optional admin note Click Approve & review plan — the normal destroy plan opens. After the admin confirms the plan, the request is marked approved and force=true destroy starts. Audit-logged as destroy-request:approve . Click Deny — the note is surfaced on the user's cluster card as a red "Destroy denied" pill (with the note in the tooltip). Audit-logged as destroy-request:deny . For limit requests, the review modal lets the admin grant the requested values or adjust them before approval. Approved values are written into the user's per-user overrides and the user receives an Activity notification. Denials can include an admin note and are audit-logged as limit-request:deny . Request emails include the requester, request id, comment, requested values, and granted values where applicable. Approval is row-locked to prevent two admins double-approving. Bypass path: admins can still force-destroy any protected cluster directly via ?force=true from the All Clusters table — useful for incident response.

title: Administration
heading: Audit Log
text: Every provisioning, scaling, upgrade, and destroy operation is recorded with user identity, operation type, cluster name, outcome, and duration — including destroy-request:* and limit-request:* events from the Requests queue. The log is append-only and filterable by user, operation, and date range.

title: Administration
heading: Resource limits
text: Limits cascade: global config sets the baseline for all users, per-user overrides take precedence when set. Limit Global default Per-user override Clusters per user Inherited from config ✅ Node pools per cluster 3 ✅ Nodes per pool 3 ✅ OCPU per node 1 ✅ RAM per node 12 GB ✅ Storage per node 50 GB ✅ Cluster tier BASIC_CLUSTER ✅ The deploy form always reflects the user's current effective limits. If a user hits a limit, the form shows a clear message with a link to contact support. Limits can be raised at any time by an admin without restarting the platform.

title: Administration
heading: Cost estimates
text: Cost estimates are visible in deployment forms, cluster cards, cluster details, templates and administrator views. They use configured resource rates with optional overrides for custom contracts. The breakdown covers the modelled compute, worker storage and control-plane components; it is not a reconciliation of your Oracle invoice. Review the rates and included components against your contract. Networking, load balancers, other services and the platform host can add charges outside the cluster estimate. Administrators can review estimated spend across active clusters. Estimates do not enforce a guaranteed monetary budget and do not include the Infrayard subscription.

title: Operations, upgrades and recovery
heading: Overview
text: You operate the Infrayard installation; Solvia Lab supplies releases, documentation and support. This page covers upgrades, backups, restores and uninstalling, with the commands to run. They are the same on OKE and k3s.

title: Operations, upgrades and recovery
heading: Responsibilities
text: Area Who Host (Kubernetes cluster or k3s VM), ingress, TLS, storage, network You OCI user, policies and keys You Backups of the database, secrets and Terraform state You Applications on the OKE clusters You Infrayard releases, release notes, documentation, support Solvia Lab

title: Operations, upgrades and recovery
heading: What to back up
text: Item Contains How PostgreSQL database infrayard Clusters, jobs, users, configuration, templates, requests, audit log, SSH keys of the worker nodes and, with the bundled Keycloak, all Keycloak users and settings Database backup , daily Terraform state bucket The state of every managed cluster Object versioning on the bucket; optionally a copy to another region Configuration values.yaml and secrets.yaml Your secret manager ( secrets.yaml ) and configuration repository ( values.yaml ) OCI API key oci_api_key.pem Your secret manager Database and state belong together: a restored database must match the clusters that actually exist in OCI. Treat backups as sensitive; they contain SSH private keys and, with the bundled Keycloak, password hashes.

title: Operations, upgrades and recovery
heading: Backups
text: The database backup is one file that contains both Infrayard and the bundled Keycloak. umask 077 kubectl exec -n infrayard infrayard-postgresql-0 -c postgresql -- \ pg_dump -U infrayard -Fc infrayard > infrayard-$(date +%F).dump Copy the files off the host, for example to an Object Storage bucket with oci os object put , and delete old ones according to your retention policy. If you use an external PostgreSQL ( postgresql.enabled: false ), back it up with your database tooling instead.

title: Operations, upgrades and recovery
heading: Restore
text: Restore into the same Infrayard version that created the backup, then upgrade if needed. Stop the services that write to the database first. BACKUP=infrayard-2026-01-31.dump # Replace with the dump to restore. test -s "$BACKUP" && kubectl scale deploy -n infrayard infrayard-api infrayard-keycloak --replicas=0 && kubectl wait --for=delete pod -n infrayard \ -l 'app.kubernetes.io/instance=infrayard,app.kubernetes.io/component in (api,keycloak)' \ --timeout=120s && kubectl exec -i -n infrayard infrayard-postgresql-0 -c postgresql -- \ pg_restore -U infrayard -d infrayard --clean --if-exists --no-owner \ --single-transaction < "$BACKUP" && kubectl scale deploy -n infrayard infrayard-api infrayard-keycloak --replicas=1 && kubectl rollout status -n infrayard deploy/infrayard-keycloak --timeout=180s && kubectl rollout status -n infrayard deploy/infrayard-api --timeout=180s Wait for the old pods to disappear before restoring so their database connections have closed. If the restore fails, PostgreSQL rolls back the transaction and the writers stay stopped. Without the bundled Keycloak, omit it from both scale commands and skip its rollout check. On a new host , start only the database first, so that nothing writes to it before the restore: install with your values and --set api.replicaCount=0 --set keycloak.replicaCount=0 , restore, then run helm upgrade with the same command without these two options. After a restore, compare the cluster list in the portal with what exists in OCI before you start new operations. A cluster created or destroyed after the backup appears in the wrong state; its Terraform state in the bucket is still correct.

title: Operations, upgrades and recovery
heading: Upgrade Infrayard
text: Before you start: Read the release notes of the target version, especially for steps marked as required. Take a database backup . Make sure no cluster operation is running ( Admin → All Clusters ). The API applies database changes automatically when it starts. They cannot be undone by downgrading; a rollback means restoring the backup. helm upgrade infrayard oci://registry.gitlab.com/solvialab/infrayard/charts/infrayard \ --version 1.5.0 -n infrayard -f values.yaml -f secrets.yaml kubectl get pods -n infrayard -w The chart version selects the image version. Changed configuration or secrets restart the affected pods automatically. After the upgrade: sign in as an administrator and as a regular user, check the cluster list and the Activity history, and run Sync in Admin → Configuration to confirm OCI access. Rollback: helm rollback infrayard -n infrayard returns the previous chart and images. If the new version had already started, also restore the backup taken before the upgrade.

title: Operations, upgrades and recovery
heading: PostgreSQL and Keycloak versions
text: The chart pins the PostgreSQL major version (currently 18) and the Keycloak version (currently 26.8). Patch releases arrive with Infrayard upgrades. A new PostgreSQL major version cannot read the old data directory. When a release moves to a new major version, its notes say so, and the upgrade needs a dump and restore: Take a database backup . Stop everything and delete the database volume: kubectl scale deploy -n infrayard infrayard-api infrayard-keycloak --replicas=0 , then kubectl delete statefulset infrayard-postgresql -n infrayard and kubectl delete pvc data-infrayard-postgresql-0 -n infrayard . Start the new version with only the database running: the helm upgrade command from above with --set api.replicaCount=0 --set keycloak.replicaCount=0 . Restore the backup with the pg_restore command. Start everything: the same helm upgrade without the two --set options. Keycloak updates its schema by itself on the first start of a new version.

title: Operations, upgrades and recovery
heading: OKE clusters are a separate topic
text: Upgrading Infrayard does not touch your OKE clusters. Kubernetes upgrades of the clusters are done per cluster in the portal; see cluster lifecycle . Plan them with worker refresh, disruption budgets and temporary extra capacity in mind.

title: Operations, upgrades and recovery
heading: Uninstall Infrayard
text: Uninstalling Infrayard does not touch the clusters it created, and only Infrayard can destroy them cleanly: their Terraform state is in the state bucket. Work through the steps in this order. Destroy the clusters you no longer need in the portal and wait until each one is destroyed. A destroyed cluster takes its compartment, VCN and node pools with it. Clusters you keep go on running and being billed. Back up the database if you may need the history later; see backups . Remove Infrayard. Helm keeps the PostgreSQL volume; deleting the claim deletes the volume as well, on OKE the 50 GB oci-bv block volume. The namespace also holds the registry and OCI key secrets: helm uninstall infrayard -n infrayard kubectl delete pvc -n infrayard data-infrayard-postgresql-0 kubectl delete namespace infrayard Remove Traefik and cert-manager if you installed them only for Infrayard in step 1 of the Kubernetes guide . When Traefik is removed, OKE deletes its load balancer. cert-manager leaves its CRDs behind; the last command deletes them: helm uninstall traefik -n traefik helm uninstall cert-manager -n cert-manager kubectl delete clusterissuer letsencrypt kubectl delete namespace traefik cert-manager kubectl get crd -o name | grep 'cert-manager.io$' | xargs kubectl delete Check OCI. On OKE, after a minute or two the load balancer is gone and the block volume is TERMINATED in the compartment of the cluster that ran Infrayard: oci lb load-balancer list -c <compartment> oci bv volume list -c <compartment> --query 'data[].{name:"display-name",state:"lifecycle-state"}' Delete the state bucket once none of its clusters is left. Versioning is on, so --empty removes every object version before the bucket: oci os bucket delete --bucket-name infrayard-tfstate --empty --force Remove the rest by hand if no other installation uses it: the DNS record of the portal, and the OCI user, group and policy from OCI setup . If you destroy the cluster that runs Infrayard, remove the load balancer and the volume first (steps 3 to 5). OKE does not delete them with the cluster: the load balancer keeps the VCN from being deleted, and the volume stays and is billed.

title: Operations, upgrades and recovery
heading: Ending a subscription
text: Ending the subscription does not stop or delete anything in OCI, and Oracle keeps billing running clusters. Before access ends, destroy the clusters you no longer need, or keep the Terraform state bucket so that they can still be managed. Details are in your agreement; see billing and licensing .

title: Troubleshooting and support
heading: Overview
text: Start with the logs. For a failed cluster operation, open the operation's Terraform log in the portal. For the installation itself: # Kubernetes kubectl get pods -n infrayard kubectl describe pod -n infrayard <pod> kubectl logs -n infrayard deploy/infrayard-api --tail=200 Note the time and the exact error before you retry, and check what actually exists in OCI before starting a second operation on the same cluster.

title: Troubleshooting and support
heading: Installation
text: Symptom Cause and fix infrayard-api pod stays in Init or ContainerCreating ; events mention infrayard-oci-key The OCI key secret is missing or in another namespace. Create it as in step 3 ImagePullBackOff , or helm show chart fails with 401 , 403 , unauthorized or denied The registry login or the regcred secret is missing, has a typo, or the token has expired. Check global.imagePullSecrets and the image addresses. If the login succeeds but pulling still fails, the token lacks read access to the registry; ask support for a new token API log or oci CLI shows 401 NotAuthenticated right after the OCI user or API key was created OCI needs a few minutes to activate a new user and key in every service. Wait five minutes and retry. If it persists, compare the fingerprint, user OCID and tenancy OCID with the API key page API log shows 404 NotAuthorizedOrNotFound for OCI calls A policy statement is missing or names the wrong group or compartment. Compare with Prepare OCI Traefik install on OKE fails with cannot unmarshal number into Go struct field ObjectMeta.metadata.annotations of type string The load balancer annotations were passed with --set , which turns 10 and 100 into numbers. Use --set-string as in step 1 Pod stays in Init:ImageInspectError ; events show short name mode is enforcing OKE nodes run CRI-O, which accepts only fully qualified image names. An image override such as postgres:18-alpine must name its registry: docker.io/library/postgres:18-alpine After a helm upgrade that fixes an image or setting, infrayard-postgresql-0 keeps its old error A StatefulSet does not replace a pod that never became ready. Delete it with kubectl delete pod -n infrayard infrayard-postgresql-0 ; it starts again with the new settings and keeps its volume helm install fails with ... is required A required value is missing, for example postgresql.auth.password or keycloak.admin.password . Add it to secrets.yaml Certificate stays READY False DNS does not point to the ingress yet, or port 80 is not reachable from the internet. Check kubectl describe certificate -n infrayard infrayard-tls and kubectl get challenges -A Sign-in shows 502 Bad Gateway or a Keycloak error page Keycloak is still starting (about a minute on the first start) or the realm import failed. Check the Keycloak logs for Realm 'infrayard' imported Keycloak does not start, log shows password authentication failed The database password changed after the first start. The database keeps the password it was created with; set the original value again

title: Troubleshooting and support
heading: Sign-in and roles
text: Symptom Cause and fix "Your account is not allowed to use Infrayard" The user lacks the access role ( requiredRole ). Assign it in Keycloak; it takes effect at the next sign-in No Admin menu The user lacks the admin role, or rolesClaim points to the wrong claim Sign-in works but data does not load The issuer setting does not match the token. See Keycloak troubleshooting A template is missing for a user The template requires a role the user does not hold A role change has no effect Roles are read from the token; the user gets the change with the next token, within the token lifetime (5 minutes by default)

title: Troubleshooting and support
heading: Missing versions or shapes
text: In Admin → Configuration , sync shapes and Kubernetes versions from OCI for the configured region. Newly found Kubernetes versions must be enabled by an administrator. A version is only offered when OCI has a node image for it and the selected shape. If the check with OCI fails, deployment is blocked on purpose. Then check the OCI user's policies and the API's outbound access. With the OCI CLI configured for the same user, this shows what OCI offers: oci ce node-pool-options get --node-pool-option-id all --region eu-frankfurt-1

title: Troubleshooting and support
heading: Existing-network validation fails
text: An existing subnet also needs its VCN OCID. The compartment must be the anchor or below it. A compartment alone does not reuse its VCN; Infrayard creates a new one. With Public endpoint restricted by CIDR allowlist on, existing VCNs and subnets are rejected. See networking .

title: Troubleshooting and support
heading: Worker nodes do not become ready
text: Look at the Terraform log and the node pool in the OCI Console. Common causes: service limits or quotas, no capacity for the shape in the availability domain, or a shape without a matching image. With your own subnet, the subnet needs a NAT gateway route and a service gateway route; without them nodes cannot register.

title: Troubleshooting and support
heading: kubectl cannot connect
text: The kubeconfig only authenticates; it does not open a network path. Check that you are on the VPN, that the cluster's endpoint mode fits your network, and that your egress range is in Allowed API CIDRs ( Admin → Configuration → OCI Settings ). Infrayard's own outbound address must be in the allowlist as well, otherwise the kubeconfig download fails; the deploy log then ends with Cluster API endpoint … not reachable from Infrayard . See step 7 of the Kubernetes guide for how to find that address.

title: Troubleshooting and support
heading: A limit blocks a request
text: Check the global default, the user's own limit and the template. Users can request more in the portal; administrators approve or adjust it in Requests . Templates may allow more than a user's limit for custom configurations.

title: Troubleshooting and support
heading: A cluster operation fails
text: Read the Terraform log, then check the resources in OCI. A failed deployment offers a cleanup action that removes partial resources; check what it will remove first. For Basic clusters, changes to nodes or a Kubernetes upgrade need a rolling worker refresh. Do not repair Infrayard-managed resources by hand in the OCI Console as a routine fix; the next Terraform run overwrites the changes. If you must intervene, contact support before running further operations on that cluster.

title: Troubleshooting and support
heading: Contact support
text: Write to support@infrayard.eu or use the support form . Include: The Infrayard version and where it runs (OKE, k3s or other Kubernetes). What you did, the approximate time and the region. The error message and the relevant log lines. Recent changes and what you have already tried. Remove private keys, tokens, passwords and personal data before you send logs. Response times and support hours are part of your subscription; see Enterprise for extended support.

text: Business includes the commercial production subscription for one production installation and one non-production test installation, released images and deployment assets, core OKE lifecycle workflows, templates, role-based access, resource limits, protected requests, cost estimates, execution logs and activity history. It includes an onboarding workshop and email support. Business support has a 48-hour response SLA during the business hours defined in the agreement. Response is not a guaranteed incident resolution time. Your order identifies the covered installations and tenancy, support calendar and authorised contacts. More installations or tenancies are arranged through Enterprise; this website does not imply unlimited installations, tenancies or managed-service resale. The customer operates the installation, OCI resources and workloads unless additional assistance is agreed. See operations and responsibilities .

heading: Evaluation
text: A paid evaluation is optional. After a demo and prerequisite review, a customer can start a monthly production subscription directly. The window starts when the agreed prerequisites are ready and the evaluation is activated. The evaluation includes a guided deployment session, time-limited registry access, the same public installation guides and business-hours email support. A single VM with k3s in your tenancy is enough; see installation . Oracle usage remains payable to Oracle. Evaluation access ends with the agreed evaluation period; production use requires a production subscription. The full evaluation fee is credited once against your first production invoice if the production order is accepted within 30 days after the evaluation ends. This applies to monthly or annual Business, qualifying Founding Business or an agreed Enterprise order. The fee is not described as a refundable deposit. Discuss an evaluation .

text: You can request an annual term after starting monthly. Agree the transition date and credit for any unused, already paid subscription time before the annual invoice is issued. The annual term then runs for twelve months from the agreed start date. A billing change does not restart the founding discount period; any founding-period transition is documented in the revised order.

title: Subscription, billing and licensing
heading: Cancellation and offboarding
text: Monthly Business can be cancelled before the next renewal by contacting hello@infrayard.eu . It ends at the close of the current paid billing period. Annual subscriptions cover the full paid twelve-month term. Refunds, Enterprise commitments and any exceptional termination rights follow the signed commercial terms. Agree offboarding before access ends, including required configuration, operational records, Terraform state and supported credential handover. Production licence rights, updates, registry access and support follow the entitlement period and the agreement. Do not assume that cancelling the software subscription deletes or stops OCI resources; Oracle usage charges continue for resources left running.

heading: Overview
text: Choose Infrayard based on capabilities available in the release delivered to your organisation. Planned work is described separately below and is not a delivery commitment unless included in a written agreement.

title: Releases and roadmap
heading: Available capabilities
text: Create, scale, upgrade, access and destroy OKE clusters through the portal. Inspect Terraform execution logs and lifecycle status. Publish cluster templates and control role visibility. Configure global limits, per-user overrides and limit-increase requests. Protect cluster destruction with an admin review workflow. Use supported existing OCI compartments, VCNs and subnets. Download Kubernetes access files without requiring local OCI CLI setup in the default access workflow. Review cost estimates, Activity notifications and audit history. Sync available shapes and Kubernetes versions with compatibility filtering. Sign in through the bundled Keycloak or your existing Keycloak. Install with Helm on Kubernetes: OKE, k3s and other distributions. Operational behaviour depends on cluster tier and network design; see requirements and cluster lifecycle .

title: Releases and roadmap
heading: Versioned delivery
text: Each release has a version number such as 1.4.0 . The Helm chart and the images of a release share that version and are published together in the private registry you receive access to; chart 1.4.0 runs images 1.4.0 . Each release is announced by e-mail to your technical contact, with release notes that list the changes and any required upgrade steps. Follow Upgrade Infrayard and run helm list -n infrayard to see which version you run. Source code and build pipelines are not needed to install or operate Infrayard.
